extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, claimants, and government officials dealing with claims against the United States for military/war-related property loss or services
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and decision-based rules governing when the United States is liable (or not) for property loss, services, occupation, salvage, medical bills, and other claims arising from military operations, occupations, or related activities. Compiles case-based principles and regulatory interpretations used to decide such claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salvage lien on United States property (The Davis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal property of the United States on board a vessel, transported from one point to another, is liable to a lien for salvage services rendered in saving the property, but such a lien cannot be enforced against the United States by suit or by in rem process when enforcement would require disturbing the possession of Government officers or agents; it may be enforced in rem only where the court's process can be enforced without disturbing Government possession, compelling the Government to appear and discharge the lien before delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Syllabus from The Davis; 2 Parsons Maritime Law, 625.) Explains limits on enforcing salvage liens against US property — practical enforcement only where possession need not be disturbed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government shipment method and general-average contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of an express stipulation to the contrary, shipment by sea as well as by rail is at carrier's risk; the Government is not required by law or regulation to ship private property of an officer by rail rather than by sea, and when public funds are involved shipments should be made in the most economical way considering time; if private property becomes subject to a general-average contribution as the result of shipment by sea, that contribution should be paid by the officer (owner), not by the Government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision Q. 20919, Jan. 16, 1907. Balances carrier-risk principles, economy of public expenditure, and responsibility for general-average contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Troops who render salvage beyond official duty may claim salvage
rubrics_metrics.description: Where troops exert themselves beyond their official duty in rescuing a vessel's cargo, they are entitled to salvage; if those engaged acquiesce, money paid for salvage may be distributed among company funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: G.12721, June 13, 1902. Distinguishes services performed strictly as official duty (no salvage) from additional efforts giving rise to salvage rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lumber cast ashore on military reservation becomes United States property; life-saving station personnel not entitled to salvage
rubrics_metrics.description: All lumber cast ashore within the limits of a military reservation ceded to the United States becomes the property of the United States, subject to claims of possible owners, regardless of whether technically 'wreck' or 'drift stuff'; services by the keeper and crew of the life-saving station and by others are not services entitling them to payment for salvage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: G.20582, Nov. 5, 1906; when such material is unsuitable for service it may be disposed of under statutory procedures (section 1241, R.S.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial-payment contract provision transfers title to United States and prevents admiralty lien
rubrics_metrics.description: A contract clause providing that parts paid for under partial payments 'shall become thereby the sole property of the United States' (but not relieving contractor of care prior to delivery) prevents a private person from obtaining an admiralty lien on the scows as against the Government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: G.3946, Nov. 5, 1907. Highlights that contractual transfer of title to the Government negates maritime lien claims by third parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of loyalty for Philippine inhabitants; burden on Government to prove disloyalty
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Philippines during the insurrection the population at large should be presumed loyal to the de jure government except where resistance is met or there is direct knowledge of disloyalty; failure to take an oath or abandonment of property are not conclusive evidence of disloyalty; accordingly, the Government bears the burden of proving an owner's disloyalty when property was taken or occupied for military purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: C.17219, Jan. 13, 1906, and related dispositions. Contrasts with treatment of inhabitants of seceding States during Civil War.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation for seizure by military necessity equals value only (no profit)
rubrics_metrics.description: When private property is seized in time of war as a military necessity and the Government undertakes to compensate the owner, the payment will be sufficient to cover the value alone, without profit to the owner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.15448, Nov. 5, 1903. Sets measure of compensation for military-necessity takings.

rubrics_metrics.name: No liability for property destroyed under military necessity or for torts of individual soldiers
rubrics_metrics.description: If animals or other property are destroyed as a matter of military necessity (authorized by applicable orders) the United States will not be liable to the owners; similarly, the United States is not liable for torts committed by individual soldiers acting without authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.18418, Dec. 22, 1905. Applies regardless of owner's sympathies; relies on General Orders and doctrine that Government not liable for officers' torts.

rubrics_metrics.name: No liability for collateral damage from lawful military measures or accidental spread without negligence
rubrics_metrics.description: When destructive acts (e.g., burning a public market by order of a commanding officer as a military measure) are performed as acts of military necessity, the United States is not liable for property destroyed in the targeted area; further, where fire accidentally spreads to adjacent property without negligence, the United States is also not liable for that collateral loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.11972, July 22, 1903. Distinguishes intended destructive acts authorized by military necessity from negligent conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seizure and use of enemy property in hostile country: no compensation; presidential instructions do not create contractual rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Private property belonging to the enemy and seized in a hostile country by way of military necessity is not compensable; instructions of the President about giving receipts, paying for taken property, or transportation do not create contractual rights against the United States in favor of the original owners and do not obligate the Government to compensate for detention or use of such enemy property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.6046, Mar. 18, 1899; C.11143, Oct. 5 & Dec. 23, 1901. Supreme Court commentary indicates proclamations cannot supersede laws of war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession/use of seized transportation by multiple powers: reimbursement and reciprocal set-off
rubrics_metrics.description: A belligerent may take forcible possession of railroads or other means of transportation and use them; when several powers operate against a common enemy, the property rights of the operating State temporarily vest in that State, transportation furnished over the road should be considered furnished by the State whose military representatives were in charge at the time, and reimbursement should be made to those representatives by the United States; reciprocal practice should be followed with credits by way of set-off for similar services rendered by the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.11107, Aug. 19, 1901. Governs inter-governmental accounting when allied or co-belligerent forces use seized infrastructure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public property occupied or damaged by troops: no implied rent obligation and no liability for torts of agents
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a municipal or other public building was occupied or burned while in possession of US troops, there was no implied obligation to pay rent for public property and the United States is not liable for torts of its agents in such circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.15318, May 7, 1906; C.26626, Apr. 30, 1910. Distinguishes public-property treatment from private-owner compensation rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation for occupied private property depends on the character of use
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination whether owners receive compensation for property occupied during an insurrection depends on circumstances: if property is used in the actual train of war (e.g., as a stronghold or fort or for preparing defenses), no compensation is due; if property is occupied in a semipermanent way for quarters or storehouses, compensation is paid as on an implied contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.16545, May 1, 1906. Practical test: 'actual train of war' (no pay) vs. semipermanent occupation (implied contract).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of owner joining insurgency on lease rights; oath of allegiance restores implied contract
rubrics_metrics.description: If the owner of leased premises joins an insurrection, the lease is abrogated and, while the owner remains an insurgent, the United States is entitled to free use of the premises as abandoned property of a public enemy; upon taking an oath of allegiance, an implied contract to pay reasonable rent arises for the period thereafter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.14994, July 28, 1903. Applies to leases during military occupations/insurrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: No reimbursement when enemy burns buildings occupied by US officers
rubrics_metrics.description: When, in time of war, a building occupied under an implied lease by United States Army officers is burned by enemies because it was occupied by American officers, the fact that owners were friendly to the US does not make the United States liable to reimburse the owner for the value of the building.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.11739, Sept. 4, 1902. Emphasizes limits on liability for hostile acts of third parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: No liability for incidental destruction of personal property during legitimate military operations; statutory limitations may bar claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For injuries to or destruction of personal property incidental to legitimate military operations in war the Government is not responsible; certain statutes (e.g., acts of Feb. 21, 1867) specially inhibited settlement of such claims arising during the Civil War and similar limitations may apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.55, 328, Jan. 20, 1888 and related decisions. Examples include cotton destroyed by explosion during possession of Mobile, AL (1865) and damage from naval bombardment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acts by military officers in civil-administration capacity may create responsibility of successor civil government (not the United States)
rubrics_metrics.description: When military authorities acting as civil administrators (e.g., during military government in the Philippines) take or use civil-government property (tearing down schoolhouse to repair road), responsibility for claims may rest with the successor local civil government (e.g., Philippine government) and not with the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.19575, May 8, 1906. Distinguishes military acts performed in civil capacity from acts of the US federal government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture/appropriation of vessels in enemy territory vests ownership in the United States; return requires Congressional authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A vessel captured by the Army in enemy territory and appropriated to Army use does not constitute a maritime capture for prize purposes; ownership passed to the United States upon capture and there is no authority to return the property except by authority of Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: G.14801, June 19, 1903; G.15693, Jan. 26, 1903. Imposes requirement of legislative action to restore ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil War 'loyal citizens' claims jurisdictional limits; relief requires express legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims for property taken from loyal citizens for use of the Union army during the Civil War were cognizable by the Southern Claims Commission but largely excluded from the Court of Claims; many such claims are barred by statute of limitations and the only relief available now is by express congressional legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P.61, 468, Oct. 3, 1893; G.2764, Nov. 27, 1896. Highlights jurisdictional/temporal barriers to redress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical bills: duty status determines Government obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical bills incurred by an officer or soldier while on leave of absence or furlough (distinct from a pass not exceeding 24 hours) are private indebtedness of the soldier and not an obligation of the Government, because the soldier is not in a duty status; however, an officer absent by verbal permit or a soldier on pass for not exceeding 24 hours is considered in duty status and medical services properly incurred while in such status are obligations of the Government. Insanity occurring while on such a short duty-status pass (not due to misconduct) preserves duty status; authorized activities (e.g., official athletic teams) likewise create Government obligation; a soldier absent without leave but taken into hospital at request of proper military authority is in 'constructive military custody' and medical bills thereafter are Government obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple decisions: G.24393 (Feb/Dec 1909, Jan 1910), C.20974, C.24398, C.16642, etc. Provides a fine-grained rule: duty status (<=24-hour pass/permit, authorized absence, hospital custody) vs. non-duty leave/furlough.

rubrics_metrics.name: United States not liable for loss/theft of personal property in military custody/hospital/company safe in the ordinary course
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a soldier's money or jewelry was turned over to wardmasters, company commanders, or stored per regulations and subsequently stolen or lost (including loss in the mail after forwarding), the United States could not be held liable for the loss in the cited decisions, although administrative recommendations (e.g., replacement by Quartermaster Dept.) may appear in records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.6269, Apr. 20, 1902; C.15157 (Aug.27,1903 & Dec.14,1906); C.25692, Oct. 23, 1909; C.12621, May 28, 1902. Distinguishes administrative remedies from legal liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on officers (including retirees in some contexts) acting as agents/attorneys in claims against the United States (sec. 5498)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 5498 R.S. punishes by fine or imprisonment any officer of the United States or person holding a place of trust who acts as agent or attorney for prosecuting claims against the United States, or otherwise aids such prosecution other than in the discharge of proper official duties; retired officers acting as agents or attorneys may be regarded as 'officers of the United States' for this section, while in other factual contexts noncommissioned retirees may not be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.20254, Aug. 20, 1906; C.18202, June 29, 1905; P.35,452, Oct. 15, 1889. Also precludes detailing an active Army officer to act as attorney for a claimant under the statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on furnishing information that could form the basis of a claim by military personnel (A.R. par. 831) with limited exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph 831 A.R. (838 of 1910) provides that no information will be furnished by any person in the military service which can be made the basis of a claim against the Government except as the regulations prescribe and to proper officers; it applies to voluntary information but does not prevent officers or soldiers from testifying when compelled by due process, nor does it prevent furnishing information in accordance with regulations (e.g., for claims under the act of May 30, 1908).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.7912 (Apr.7,1900; Feb.8,1910); G.O.163 W.D. Sept. 21, 1906. Also notes disciplinary measures and cross-reference to sec. 5498.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of statutory disqualification for rebellion (sec. 3480): personal disability only
rubrics_metrics.description: The provision of section 3480 R.S. making it unlawful to pay certain claims to persons who promoted the late rebellion created a personal disability only and could not operate against the heirs of parties thus disqualified unless the heirs themselves participated in the rebellion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.39, J17, Feb. 7, 1878. Clarifies reach of statutory disqualifications on succession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of private vessels by officers acting as relief agents does not create US liability
rubrics_metrics.description: When a private steamer was used for relief work and received orders from Army and Navy officers acting as relief agents (not as representatives of the United States), the United States was held not liable to the owners for compensation for the use of the vessel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.20652, Mar. 4 & Apr. 2, 1907. Distinguishes relief-agent authority from official federal authority to bind the United States.

rubrics_metrics.name: No Government liability for counsel fees or related expenses in court-martial matters and certain witness expenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims against the United States by an attorney for services rendered as counsel for an accused officer in a court-martial trial are without merit as against the United States; likewise, no provision of law supports payment of time, cost, and expenses incurred by a claimant in traveling to collect fees due a civilian witness before a court-martial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P.32,165, May 2, 1899; C.1807, Nov. 2, 1895. Distinguishes individual legal expenses from Government obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: No claim for pay/damages for detention awaiting military trial or mistaken detention on suspicion of desertion
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier, although later discharged, has no claim against the United States for pay as damages for a period during which he was, though innocent, detained awaiting trial for a military offense and action on the proceedings; similarly a civilian wrongfully detained on reasonable suspicion of being a deserter has no legal claim for damages against the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P.42,375, Aug. 23, 1890; P.43,145, Oct. 4, 1890. Establishes nonliability for detention in these military procedural contexts.
